# Alkalis (potash, soda, caustic lye) (`alkali_soda`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/chemistry.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Chemistry (`chemistry`)
- Deps: helped by lime_burning, sulphuric_acid, salt_production
- Core idea: Potash is got by leaching wood ash with water and boiling the liquor dry in an iron pot (about 1 kg from 500–1000 kg of wood); soda comes from natron lakes or from the ash of salt-marsh plants (barilla), and the two are different substances. Either becomes caustic, and far stronger, when its solution is stirred with slaked lime and poured off the chalk that settles. Leblanc's route makes soda from salt: salt and sulphuric acid give salt cake, which is roasted with limestone and coal and then leached. Solvay's route passes ammonia and carbon dioxide into brine. Alkali is needed for soap, glass, paper, bleaching and dyeing.
- Pitfalls:
  - Caustic lye destroys eyes and skin; aluminium, tin and zinc vessels dissolve in it.
  - Treating potash and soda as the same; potash gives soft soap and a different glass.
  - Leblanc works vent hydrochloric acid gas and leave stinking sulphide waste that ruined whole districts.
  - Believing sea salt and water alone give soda; salt must be chemically converted.
- History: egypt: from c. 3000 BC – natron from Wadi Natrun for mummification, cleaning, faience and glass; mesopotamia: from c. 2500 BC – plant ash alkali for soap, dyeing and glass; china: by Han times – plant ash lye and natural soda (jian) for degumming silk, dyeing and food; islamic: 8th–13th c. – plant ash (al-qali, hence 'alkali') from Syria supplies glass and soap makers; causticising with lime described; europe: medieval – potash from forest ash; 1736 Duhamel distinguishes soda from potash; 1791 Leblanc process; 1861–1865 Solvay process; 1890s electrolytic caustic soda; americas: 1790 – the first United States patent is for a potash process (Samuel Hopkins)
- Read:
  - Archibald Clow & Nan L. Clow, The Chemical Revolution (1952)
  - L. F. Haber, The Chemical Industry during the Nineteenth Century (1958)
